nodes.title: Command-line tooling: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Most exam workflows involve `aws`, `az`, `gcloud`, or `kubectl`. Knowing the structure of each (resource → command → flags) saves you in the lab portion and in real life. They're all roughly the same shape with different naming conventions.

flashcards.front: How do you authenticate the AWS CLI?
flashcards.back: `aws configure` writes credentials to `~/.aws/credentials` (access key + secret) and `~/.aws/config` (region, output format). Use named profiles for multi-account: `aws s3 ls --profile prod`. Prefer `aws configure sso` or temporary STS credentials over long-lived access keys.

flashcards.front: What does `kubectl get` do, and what flags are essential?
flashcards.back: Lists resources of a kind: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl get nodes`. Key flags: `-n <namespace>` (default is `default`), `-o wide` (more columns), `-o yaml` (full manifest), `--watch` (live updates), `-l label=value` (filter by label).

flashcards.front: Output formatting — JSON, table, text?
flashcards.back: AWS / Azure / gcloud all support `--output json|text|table|yaml`. JSON is for piping into `jq` for scripts. Table is for humans browsing in the terminal. Always set a default in your config so you don't squint at JSON when browsing.

flashcards.front: How do you find a command's options without leaving the terminal?
flashcards.back: `aws <service> <command> help` (or `--help`), `kubectl <verb> --help`, `az <group> <command> --help`. These open built-in docs with every flag listed. Searching the official web docs is for concepts; for syntax, the local help is always current.

nodes.title: Dockerfiles and image building: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building a container image — a sequence of instructions that produce immutable, layered, portable artifacts. The exam wants you to know which instructions create layers, how the cache works, and how to keep images small and secure.

flashcards.front: Which Dockerfile instructions create a new layer?
flashcards.back: RUN, COPY, ADD each create a new read-only layer in the image. CMD, ENTRYPOINT, ENV, WORKDIR, EXPOSE update image metadata but don't create layers. Layer count affects image size and build cache hit rate.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage builds — what's the point?
flashcards.back: First stage installs build tools (compilers, package managers) and produces an artifact. Second stage copies ONLY the artifact into a minimal runtime image. Final image is tiny (no build deps) and surface-area for vulnerabilities is small. Standard pattern for Go, Java, Node production builds.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
flashcards.back: ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs. CMD provides default arguments (overridable at `docker run` time). The two combine: ENTRYPOINT ["nginx"] + CMD ["-g", "daemon off;"]. Override at runtime: `docker run myimg -h` runs `nginx -h`. Use ENTRYPOINT to lock in 'what this container IS'.

flashcards.front: Why pin base image versions instead of `:latest`?
flashcards.back: `latest` is a moving target — your build is non-reproducible. Today's `python:latest` might be 3.12; next month it's 3.13 and your code breaks subtly. Pin to a specific tag (`python:3.12-slim`) or, for compliance, a digest (`python@sha256:...`). Update intentionally, not by accident.

nodes.title: Docker Swarm (DCA): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in container orchestrator — simpler than Kubernetes, natively integrated with the Docker CLI. The DCA exam tests manager/worker topology, service definitions, overlay networks for cross-node communication, and Raft consensus for leader election.

flashcards.front: Manager node vs worker node — what does each do?
flashcards.back: Manager nodes maintain cluster state using Raft consensus, schedule tasks onto workers, and serve the Swarm API (docker service commands). Worker nodes receive task assignments from managers and run the containers. Managers can also run workloads unless `--availability=drain` excludes them. A Swarm should have an odd number of managers (1, 3, 5) — Raft needs (N/2)+1 quorum to elect a leader.

flashcards.front: What is a Swarm service vs a task?
flashcards.back: A service is the desired-state declaration: image, replicas, ports, resources (e.g., `docker service create --replicas 3 nginx`). A task is one running instance of the service assigned to a specific node — it maps to a single container. If a task fails, Swarm schedules a replacement. Services are the unit you manage; tasks are what Swarm creates automatically.

flashcards.front: Overlay network — what problem does it solve in Swarm?
flashcards.back: Containers on different nodes have different docker0 bridge IPs — they can't talk to each other natively. An overlay network creates a virtual L2 network spanning all nodes using VXLAN encapsulation. Containers attached to the same overlay network can reach each other by service name via Swarm's built-in DNS; traffic is encrypted with AES-256 when you add `--opt encrypted`.

flashcards.front: Raft consensus — how many managers can you lose before the cluster is unavailable?
flashcards.back: Raft requires a majority (quorum) of managers to be reachable. With 3 managers, quorum = 2; you can lose 1. With 5 managers, quorum = 3; you can lose 2. If quorum is lost, Swarm stops accepting cluster state changes (new service deploys fail) but existing containers keep running. Recover by restarting lost managers or force-promoting a worker.

questions.q: An admin wants to bootstrap the very first manager of a new Swarm cluster on the current host: initialize the Raft cluster, generate join tokens for future managers and workers, and become the leader. Which command does this?
choices: docker swarm create --advertise-addr <ip>
docker cluster create --mode manager
docker swarm start --manager
docker swarm init [--advertise-addr <ip>]
questions.explanation: `docker swarm init` bootstraps the Swarm on the current node, promotes it to manager and Raft leader, and prints the `docker swarm join --token …` commands for worker and manager nodes; `--advertise-addr` is added when the host has more than one interface. `docker swarm create` and `docker swarm start` are not real subcommands — the create/start verbs exist for services, not the swarm itself. `docker cluster create` is not a Docker CLI verb either; Swarm's bootstrap primitive is spelled `swarm init`.

questions.q: In Docker Swarm terminology, how do a service and a task differ?
choices: A service declares desired state — image, replicas, ports, constraints — and a task is one running container instance the scheduler creates to satisfy that state
A task is the persistent Raft record of the workload while the service is a stateless CLI wrapper that only exists during the create-or-update call
A service is defined to run exactly one container, while a task is a scheduling group that bundles multiple replicas of that container together on one node
Service and task are two aliases for the same Swarm object; the label used depends on whether the object is being created, inspected, or scaled
questions.explanation: A service is the declarative unit — image, replica count, networks, constraints, update policy — and the manager decomposes it into tasks, each of which is one scheduled container instance on a specific node. It is the tasks that are ephemeral: when one dies, the manager creates a new task to keep the replica count at the desired level. Persistent Raft state lives on the manager quorum, not inside tasks, so the second option is inverted. A service can have many replicas (or run globally on every node), so 'exactly one container' is wrong. And service and task are two different objects with different subcommands (`docker service`, `docker service ps`), not synonyms.

questions.q: A Swarm service called `webapp` currently runs three replicas and needs to run five. Which command scales it to the new replica count?
choices: docker swarm scale webapp 5
docker service resize webapp --replicas=5
docker service update webapp --count=5
docker service scale webapp=5
questions.explanation: `docker service scale webapp=5` sets the replica count; several services can be scaled in one call (`docker service scale a=3 b=5`), and the manager schedules new tasks or terminates surplus ones. `docker swarm scale` is not a real subcommand — scaling is a service operation, not a swarm-level one. `docker service resize` does not exist. `docker service update --count=5` uses the wrong flag; the correct spelling is `--replicas=5`, which is also a valid but less compact alternative to `service scale`.

questions.q: A `docker service update` rollout is in progress and new tasks are failing. Without intervention, Swarm keeps replacing healthy old tasks with broken new ones. Which flag pauses the rolling update on failure so the operator can investigate?
choices: --failure-action=stop
--update-failure-action=pause
--rollback-on-failure=true
--update-policy=halt
questions.explanation: `--update-failure-action=pause` halts the rolling update when the failure ratio is exceeded, letting the operator triage before more old tasks are replaced; the alternative values are `continue` (default) and `rollback`. `--failure-action` (without `update-`) does not exist for `service update`. `--rollback-on-failure` is not a real flag; automatic rollback is achieved with `--update-failure-action=rollback`, plus the separate `--rollback-*` tuning flags. `--update-policy=halt` is invented — there is no `--update-policy` flag in the Docker CLI.

questions.q: A Swarm monitoring agent must run exactly one task on every node currently in the cluster and on any node that joins later. Which Swarm service mode achieves that?
choices: A federated-service mode that spreads work across separate Swarm clusters
Global mode — the scheduler runs exactly one task on every Active node in the Swarm
An external-IP mode that assigns each node's task a routable public IP
An unlimited-replicas mode that scales freely across all nodes without a target count
questions.explanation: Global-mode services run exactly one task per Active node — as nodes join, tasks are scheduled on them automatically; as nodes leave, their tasks are cleaned up. This is the closest analogue to Kubernetes DaemonSets. There is no federated mode across separate clusters — Swarm has no built-in multi-cluster federation. There is no `external-IP mode`; publishing is controlled via `--publish` on services, not a service mode. `Unlimited replicas` is not a valid mode: services are either replicated (with a fixed replica count) or global.

questions.q: A Swarm with 5 managers loses 3 of them at once. Which statement best describes what happens to the cluster?
choices: Losing any single manager immediately halts scheduling and blocks all writes because Raft consensus cannot tolerate the failure of even one voting manager in a 5-node quorum
Worker nodes automatically self-promote to managers whenever Raft quorum is lost, restoring the (N/2)+1 majority within seconds without any operator involvement
In Swarm, managers only run workload tasks while workers handle Raft consensus and scheduling — so with 3 workers still alive the cluster remains fully writable
The remaining managers lack the (N/2)+1 quorum, so no new state changes can be committed — existing tasks keep running but no new services, updates, or scaling operations can succeed
questions.explanation: Raft requires (N/2)+1 managers for a write quorum. With 5 managers configured, quorum is 3; losing 3 leaves 2 healthy managers, so the cluster becomes read-only. Existing tasks keep running because the workers already have their instructions, but no new services, updates, scaling, or node changes can be committed until quorum is restored. The 'single-manager failure halts scheduling' claim is false — 5 managers tolerate 2 failures cleanly. Workers do not auto-promote; promotion is an explicit manager operation and is impossible without quorum. Raft consensus and scheduling live on the managers, not on the workers, so the third option inverts the architecture.

questions.q: A Swarm service needs an environment-specific nginx.conf that differs between dev, staging, and prod. The file is not sensitive but should be managed centrally in Swarm and mounted into the container as a file — without rebuilding the image. Which Swarm feature fits?
choices: An NFS bind mount populated by a Puppet run on each Swarm node
An ENV instruction in the Dockerfile that inlines the config text at build time
Docker Configs — non-sensitive configuration objects stored in Swarm and mounted as files at a target path in each task
Per-environment images tagged nginx:dev, nginx:staging, nginx:prod that each embed the appropriate config
questions.explanation: Docker Configs are the direct answer: `docker config create` stores the file in the Swarm's Raft log, and `docker service create --config source=...,target=...` mounts it inside each task at the chosen path, exactly like Secrets but without encryption. NFS bind mounts can also work but are managed outside Swarm and impose external infrastructure. Baking config into ENV at build time couples config changes to image rebuilds and does not deliver a file, which the requirement calls for. Per-environment images are an anti-pattern: they diverge from the immutable-image-with-external-config principle and defeat the point of one image per binary.

questions.q: In Docker Swarm, the default ingress overlay network enables the routing mesh. Which statement best describes what that means?
choices: Any Swarm node accepts connections on a service's published port and routes them via ingress+IPVS to a healthy task, regardless of which node the task runs on
It is the manager control-plane Raft overlay that carries manager-to-manager consensus traffic between Swarm managers and is disabled on worker nodes by default
It is a dedicated metrics-collection overlay that carries container health and telemetry data from every worker node up to the Swarm managers for aggregation
It is an external load-balancer integration overlay that offloads all L4 load balancing for published ports to a configured cloud provider's managed LB
questions.explanation: The ingress network is what makes the Swarm routing mesh work: every node listens on each service's published port and, if the local node has no task for that service, forwards the connection over the ingress overlay + IPVS to a node that does. That is why a single external load balancer can point at any Swarm node IP. Raft traffic between managers rides a separate control-plane connection, not the ingress overlay. There is no metrics-collection overlay by design in Swarm — metrics ride whatever telemetry driver you plug in. And ingress is not an external LB integration; it is an internal, in-cluster L4 load balancer built on IPVS.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: By default, `docker run nginx` attaches the new container to a single-host network that uses a Linux bridge plus iptables NAT for outbound traffic and port publishing for inbound. Which built-in network driver provides that behavior?
choices: The none driver, which leaves the container with only a loopback interface
The bridge driver, backed by the docker0 Linux bridge and iptables NAT
The overlay driver, which builds a multi-host VXLAN network for Swarm services
The host driver, which shares the host's network namespace with the container
questions.explanation: The bridge driver is Docker's default single-host driver: it plugs each container into the docker0 Linux bridge, gives it a private RFC1918 IP, and uses iptables NAT to reach the internet or publish ports. The none driver removes all connectivity — not the default and not the described behavior. The overlay driver is a multi-host Swarm construct built on VXLAN, not the default per-container network. The host driver shares the host's network namespace entirely, so there is no isolated bridge or NAT — exactly the opposite of what the question describes.

questions.q: Two containers on a user-defined bridge can reach each other by container name (`ping web`), but the same two containers on the default `bridge` network cannot. Why does name resolution work on user-defined bridges but not on the default bridge?
choices: User-defined bridges ship with an embedded DNS server that resolves container names; the default bridge does not
The default bridge is IPv6-only, so IPv4-only container names cannot resolve on it
Name resolution between containers requires Docker Compose to be installed
Name-based resolution does work on the default bridge; the operator has simply misconfigured DNS
questions.explanation: User-defined bridges include Docker's embedded DNS resolver (127.0.0.11) that maps container names and aliases to IPs; the default `bridge` network was kept in its legacy behavior and relies on the deprecated `--link` flag or explicit IPs for cross-container discovery. The default bridge is dual-stack when IPv6 is enabled — it is not IPv6-only, and the IPv4/IPv6 distinction is unrelated to name resolution. Compose is not required; it only sets up user-defined networks under the hood. Claiming that resolution 'does work' on the default bridge contradicts documented Docker behavior.

questions.q: A Swarm cluster has replicas of a service spread across three managers and five workers. The replicas must communicate as if they were on the same Layer-2 broadcast domain even though they run on different hosts. Which network driver satisfies that requirement?
choices: The host driver, which attaches each container directly to the host network
The overlay driver, which encapsulates traffic between Swarm nodes with VXLAN
A CDN-backed network driver that routes container traffic through an edge PoP
A single-node encrypted network driver scoped to one host at a time
questions.explanation: The overlay driver builds a multi-host virtual L2 network by wrapping frames in VXLAN and sending them between Swarm nodes over the underlay; containers on different hosts see one another as if on the same LAN. The host driver only removes network isolation on a single node and does nothing to bridge separate hosts. There is no CDN-backed built-in network driver; CDNs sit outside the container network model entirely. A single-node encrypted network is a contradiction — Docker does support `--opt encrypted`, but only on overlay networks that already span nodes, not on a per-host driver.

questions.q: A container must run with no external connectivity whatsoever — no DNS, no outbound, no inbound — with only a loopback interface inside. Which network driver satisfies that requirement?
choices: The bridge driver with --icc=false, which blocks inter-container traffic on the same bridge
The none driver, which gives the container only a loopback interface and no other links
A driver named 'isolated', which disables ingress on the default network
The host driver, which shares the host's network namespace with the container
questions.explanation: The none driver attaches no interfaces beyond `lo`, so the container cannot reach anything and nothing can reach it — exactly the required air-gapped shape. `--icc=false` only blocks container-to-container traffic on a bridge, leaving external and inbound access intact via NAT and port publishing. There is no built-in driver called `isolated`; that name does not resolve to any of Docker's network drivers. The host driver is the opposite of isolation: the container shares every host interface, so it can reach and be reached across the whole network.

questions.q: A running container `web` is on the `frontend` network. The admin wants to attach it to a `backend` network as well without stopping and recreating it. Which command does that?
choices: docker container network-add web backend
docker run --network=backend web
docker network connect backend web
docker network join backend web
questions.explanation: `docker network connect <network> <container>` attaches an already-running container to an additional network and gives it a new interface and IP on that network; `docker network disconnect` is the inverse. `docker container network-add` is not a real subcommand. `docker run --network=…` sets the network for a brand-new container, not for one that is already running. `docker network join` is not a real subcommand either — the analogous verb (`swarm join`) belongs to the `swarm` object, not `network`.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.front: What is the CIA triad?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.

flashcards.front: What does 'least privilege' mean?
flashcards.back: Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.

flashcards.front: What is defense in depth?
flashcards.back: Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: Docker Content Trust (DCT), when enabled via `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1`, causes Docker to accept only image tags that carry a valid publisher signature. Which of the following best describes what DCT actually does?
choices: Encrypts image layers server-side in the registry so their bytes cannot be read while the image sits at rest between push and pull
Requires the pulling user to complete two-factor authentication (TOTP or WebAuthn) at the CLI before Docker will begin the pull
Uses digital signatures over image manifests (backed by Notary/TUF) so tampering after publication is detected on pull
Scans images for known CVE vulnerabilities and blocks any image that has an unfixed critical or high finding from being pulled or run
questions.explanation: DCT signs image tags with keys managed by Notary (built on The Update Framework); on pull, Docker verifies the signature before accepting the image, so tampering or MITM substitution after publication is caught. DCT does not encrypt layers — registries and clients can still see the layer bytes, they simply verify the signature. DCT does not add 2FA on the user account; it authenticates the publisher, not the pulling user. Vulnerability scanning is a separate feature offered by Docker Scout, Snyk, Trivy, or registry-native scanners; DCT is a signing framework, not a scanner.

questions.q: A Swarm service needs a database password. It must be encrypted at rest in the Swarm state and delivered to the container as an in-memory file under `/run/secrets/`, never persisted on disk or bakeable into the image. Which feature meets that requirement?
choices: Docker Secrets — encrypted in the Raft log, mounted as tmpfs at /run/secrets in target containers only
Hard-coding the password with an ENV instruction in the Dockerfile at build time
Passing the password as a plain environment variable in the compose file's environment: block
Mounting a host directory that contains a password file into the container as a bind mount
questions.explanation: Docker Secrets store the secret encrypted in Swarm's Raft log, ship it to authorized nodes over mTLS, and expose it inside the container as a tmpfs-backed file at `/run/secrets/<name>` — never on disk on the worker. Hard-coding via ENV bakes the secret into every image layer and is visible through `docker history` and `docker inspect`. Compose-style environment variables travel through the process environment and are readable with `docker inspect`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, and many logs. A bind mount from the host keeps the secret in plaintext on every worker's disk and outside Docker's access-controlled distribution mechanism.

questions.q: A container must bind to port 80 but should not have any other root privileges on the host kernel. What is the recommended least-privilege pattern for that container?
choices: Run with --privileged and rely on the seccomp profile to block dangerous syscalls at runtime
Remove AppArmor and seccomp profiles so only capabilities gate what the process can do
Drop all Linux capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL and add back only --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE
Disable networking with --network=none and disable the mount namespace so bind(2) succeeds anyway
questions.explanation: Dropping ALL capabilities and re-adding only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` is the classical least-privilege pattern: the process keeps the exact power it needs (bind to a port below 1024) and nothing else. `--privileged` is the opposite — it disables namespaces, capability dropping, and the default seccomp profile. Removing AppArmor and seccomp weakens the defense-in-depth around capabilities rather than tightening it. Disabling networking with `--network=none` breaks the requirement to serve on port 80, and namespace changes cannot substitute for CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE.

questions.q: A defense-in-depth pattern runs a container with its root filesystem mounted read-only; the app writes only to tmpfs and volumes. Which `docker run` flag enables that?
choices: --read-only, which makes the container's root filesystem read-only
--image-read-only, which pins the source image to a read-only registry copy
--isolate-writes, which prevents other containers from reading this container's filesystem
--config-immutable, which prevents runtime changes to the container's configuration
questions.explanation: `docker run --read-only` mounts the container's rootfs read-only; combine with `--tmpfs /tmp` (and named volumes for real state) so the app still has writable scratch and persistent storage. It hardens the container against write-based persistence and log tampering after an intrusion. `--image-read-only` is invented — images in the local content store are already immutable and Docker has no such flag. `--isolate-writes` and `--config-immutable` are also invented flags. The specific defense-in-depth pattern in the question maps directly to `--read-only`.

questions.q: Docker applies a default seccomp profile to every container. Which of the following best describes what seccomp does?
choices: It encrypts inter-container traffic on overlay networks between Swarm nodes
It restricts which Linux syscalls a container's processes are allowed to invoke
It restricts which Docker CLI commands each host user is authorized to run
It rate-limits the container's network bandwidth and shapes egress QoS
questions.explanation: seccomp (secure computing mode) is a kernel syscall filter; Docker's default profile blocks about 44 dangerous syscalls (like `kexec_load`, `reboot`, `add_key`) and allows the rest, and custom profiles can tighten it further. Encrypting overlay traffic is done with `--opt encrypted` on the overlay network, unrelated to seccomp. Restricting CLI commands per host user is the job of Docker authorization plugins (via `--authorization-plugin`), not seccomp. Network bandwidth shaping is handled by cgroups and tc; seccomp filters syscalls and has no bandwidth knob.

nodes.title: Docker build and image layers: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Docker builds images layer by layer from a Dockerfile. Understanding the layer cache, multi-stage builds, and build context is essential for DCA exam questions on image size and build performance.

flashcards.front: What triggers a cache miss during docker build?
flashcards.back: Any change to a Dockerfile instruction or the files it COPYs invalidates that layer and all subsequent layers — order instructions from least to most frequently changed.

flashcards.front: Multi-stage build — main benefit?
flashcards.back: Compile or test in one stage using a full SDK image, then COPY only the binary/artifact into a minimal final stage — dramatically reduces final image size.

flashcards.front: docker build --no-cache — when to use?
flashcards.back: Forces a full rebuild from scratch, ignoring the layer cache. Useful when you need the latest base image or a fresh dependency fetch despite no Dockerfile changes.

flashcards.front: .dockerignore — purpose?
flashcards.back: Excludes files from the build context sent to the Docker daemon. Reduces build time and prevents accidentally baking secrets or large dev files into the image.

questions.q: A repository holds a large `node_modules/`, `.git/`, and log files next to the Dockerfile. `docker build .` currently ships all of them to the daemon as build context. Which mechanism excludes files from being sent to the daemon in the first place?
choices: A .dockerignore file at the build-context root
Setting the excluded paths as hidden environment variables at build time
Adding an EXCLUDE instruction to the Dockerfile so those paths are skipped
Blocking the affected paths in the daemon's registry pull policy
questions.explanation: The `.dockerignore` file at the root of the build context tells the CLI which paths to strip before sending the tarball to the daemon, keeping the context small and preventing secrets or huge directories from being uploaded. Environment variables have no bearing on which files are packaged into the build context — they configure processes, not the context filter. There is no EXCLUDE Dockerfile instruction; ignoring context files must happen client-side. The registry pull policy controls how images are fetched from a registry, not what the local CLI sends into a build.

questions.q: A Go service compiles to a 50 MB static binary but the Go toolchain adds 800 MB. Which technique lets a single Dockerfile produce a small runtime image that contains only the compiled binary?
choices: Parallel-image builds where multiple FROM instructions each compile a different image concurrently
A multi-stage build where later FROM stages COPY only the artifacts they need from earlier build stages
Cross-platform builds where multiple FROM instructions target different OS/arch pairs simultaneously
Conditional builds where multiple FROM instructions branch on if/else logic during compile
questions.explanation: A multi-stage build uses several FROM directives inside one Dockerfile; the runtime stage starts from a minimal base image and COPYs only the compiled binary out of a heavier build stage, keeping the final image tiny. The 'parallel images' option is wrong because a Dockerfile produces exactly one tagged output image, not one per FROM. Multi-stage is unrelated to cross-platform builds — those use `--platform` and buildx, not FROM chaining. Dockerfiles have no if/else construct; conditional logic must be handled by build args or external tooling, not by FROM.

questions.q: A Dockerfile puts `COPY package.json ./` before `RUN npm install` and `COPY . .` afterwards. What behavior of the Docker build cache does this ordering exploit?
choices: Docker caches the whole image as a single opaque unit and only rebuilds it when the base image referenced in FROM changes or is repulled
Docker caches RUN instructions but always rebuilds any COPY instruction because file bytes are considered volatile, so ordering does not affect cache reuse
Each instruction is cached individually and a cache miss on any instruction invalidates the cache for that instruction and every subsequent instruction
Docker caches its builds by tag: any change to a Dockerfile is re-cached under a new automatically incremented tag so previous build work is retained under the old tag
questions.explanation: The Docker build cache is per-instruction and sequential: if `COPY package.json` and its inputs are unchanged, `RUN npm install` above it stays cached; but as soon as any instruction (or its inputs) changes, that layer and every subsequent layer are rebuilt. That is exactly why frequently changing content (`COPY . .`) goes near the end. There is no whole-image cache tied only to FROM changes; content of intermediate instructions is what invalidates. COPY steps are cached the same way RUN steps are — Docker hashes the copied file set. And tag-based caching is not how the layer cache works.

questions.q: BuildKit is Docker's modern build engine (default in current Docker versions and enabled by `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` on older ones). Which of the following statements best describes BuildKit?
choices: BuildKit is Docker's replacement for Docker Compose as the runtime orchestrator for multi-container applications; it can execute a docker-compose.yml file directly against a single host without any Compose binary installed, and picks up service definitions automatically

BuildKit runs only on Windows Server hosts and is used exclusively for building Windows-based container images from Dockerfiles that begin with `FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/*`; on Linux hosts the legacy builder is still the only supported build subsystem

BuildKit is a commercial-only add-on shipped with Docker Business and Docker Enterprise; it requires a per-builder-node paid license to unlock its concurrent build steps, cache mounts, and secret and SSH mount features on Linux and Windows

BuildKit is Docker's newer build subsystem, adding parallel build steps, per-stage caching, `RUN --mount=type=secret` and `type=ssh`, cross-platform builds via `--platform`, and shared caches via `RUN --mount=type=cache`
questions.explanation: BuildKit is the modern build subsystem (LLB-based) shipped with Docker; its notable features are exactly the ones listed: parallel steps across stages, better caching, build-time secret and SSH mounts that never persist into layers, cross-platform builds via `--platform`, and reusable cache mounts. It has nothing to do with orchestrating containers — that is Compose/Swarm's job. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows hosts and builds both Linux and Windows images. It is open source and free; no paid Docker EE license is required to use it.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A MySQL container's data must survive container restarts, container removal, daemon restart, and host reboot, and its storage should be managed by Docker rather than pinned to a specific host path. Which storage type fits?
choices: The container's own writable layer at /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff
A named Docker volume created with docker volume create
A tmpfs mount targeted at /var/lib/mysql
A bind mount from /tmp on the host into the container
questions.explanation: A named volume is stored under Docker's control, persists independently of any container, and can be reattached to a new container after removal — exactly what a database needs. The writable layer is discarded when the container is removed, so it fails requirement (b). A tmpfs mount lives in RAM and evaporates whenever the container stops, which fails every requirement except restart-in-place. A bind mount to `/tmp` is not Docker-managed and, on most Linux distributions, `/tmp` is cleaned at boot (via systemd-tmpfiles), so the database would be wiped on host reboot.

questions.q: Which statement most accurately captures the practical difference between a bind mount and a named Docker volume?
choices: Docker volumes are strictly read-only inside the container by design; bind mounts are the only mount type that supports read-write access to persistent host data
Bind mounts are available only on Linux hosts; Docker volumes are the only mount type that works on Windows and macOS Docker installations
A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container and is tied to that path; a Docker volume is managed by Docker with its own lifecycle and works with volume drivers
Bind mounts are strictly faster than named Docker volumes because bind-mounted paths bypass Docker's storage stack and hit the host filesystem directly
questions.explanation: The defining distinction is management and portability: a bind mount pins the container to a specific host path, while a Docker volume is created and located by Docker itself and can be backed by pluggable drivers (NFS, EBS, and so on). Read-only vs read-write is orthogonal — both mount types support `:ro` and are read-write by default. Bind mounts work on Windows and macOS hosts (with path translation) and Docker volumes work everywhere too, so the OS-only claim is false. On Linux, both mount types write to a host filesystem with equivalent performance; performance is not a defining bind-vs-volume distinction.

questions.q: A container needs a fast scratch directory that lives entirely in RAM, never touches host disk, and is wiped as soon as the container stops. Which mount type fits?
choices: A compressed overlay-filesystem mount over the image's read-only layers
A read-only bind mount from a host directory into the container's scratch path
A tmpfs mount at the scratch path
A persistent BuildKit cache mount that is reused across image builds
questions.explanation: A tmpfs mount is backed by the host's RAM and never lands on disk; when the container stops the tmpfs area is torn down, matching every requirement. An overlay mount over the image layers is the container's normal writable layer — it lives on disk and grows with writes, and it is not addressable as its own mount type in `docker run`. A read-only bind mount cannot serve as scratch space because writes are forbidden. A BuildKit cache mount is a build-time construct, not a runtime container mount, and it deliberately persists across builds.

questions.q: An admin needs to cap a container at 1.5 CPUs and 512 MB of memory. Which Linux kernel subsystem does Docker use to meter and enforce those resource limits per container?
choices: Linux namespaces, which give the container isolated PID, network, mount, and UTS views
seccomp, which filters the set of syscalls that the container's processes are allowed to make
SELinux/AppArmor MAC, which restricts file and process access via mandatory access control
Control groups (cgroups), which meter and enforce CPU, memory, block I/O, and PID limits per process group
questions.explanation: cgroups are the kernel subsystem that measures and constrains CPU shares/quotas, memory, block I/O, PIDs, and network bandwidth per process group; `docker run --cpus=1.5 --memory=512m` translates directly into cgroup settings. Namespaces provide the isolation dimension (separate PID trees, network stacks, mount tables), not the metering dimension. seccomp is a syscall filter and cannot limit CPU or memory usage. SELinux and AppArmor implement mandatory access control over files and syscalls; they do not throttle resources.

questions.q: A container sees its own PID 1, its own network interfaces, its own filesystem root, and its own hostname — separate from the host's. Which Linux kernel feature provides those isolated views?
choices: Control groups (cgroups v1/v2), which meter and enforce CPU shares and quotas, memory ceilings, block I/O, and PID counts per container process group
AppArmor, which applies per-process mandatory access control policies over file paths and syscalls and can restrict what a container's processes may open
seccomp (secure computing mode), which filters the set of Linux syscalls that a process is allowed to make and is applied by Docker via a default profile
Linux namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, UTS, IPC, USER, CGROUP), which give each container its own view of kernel resources
questions.explanation: Namespaces are the kernel primitive that produces isolated views: PID namespace for process IDs, NET namespace for network stacks, MNT namespace for filesystem mounts, UTS for hostname, IPC for shared memory, USER for UID mapping. cgroups do resource metering and enforcement, not isolation — they answer 'how much', not 'what can I see'. AppArmor is a Linux MAC layer for files and syscalls; it does not create isolated PID trees or network stacks. seccomp filters syscalls but does not give a process its own PID tree, network stack, or filesystem root.

questions.q: A junior engineer asks whether a Docker image and a Docker container are the same object. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the two?
choices: An image is a read-only stack of filesystem layers; a container is a running (or stopped) instance of that image with a writable top layer and its own namespaces
An image and a container are two names for the same runtime artifact; the term used depends on whether the artifact is idle or executing
An image is the packaging format used in development while a container is the packaging format used in production; they share no other technical distinction
A container is the on-disk representation stored under /var/lib/docker while an image is the in-memory copy loaded when execution begins
questions.explanation: An image is an immutable, layered filesystem snapshot; a container is a live instance created from that image with an extra thin writable layer and its own PID/network/mount namespaces. The 'two names for the same thing' answer is wrong because containers add runtime state (writable layer, namespaces, cgroups) that an image lacks. Splitting them by 'dev vs prod' invents a distinction that does not exist — the same image runs everywhere. Claiming the container lives on disk while the image is in memory inverts reality: image layers sit on disk in the graph driver's storage, and only the running process view is loaded into memory.

questions.q: Which of the following most accurately describes the relationship between a Docker registry and Docker Hub?
choices: A registry is the server-side storage and distribution system for images; Docker Hub is one specific public registry operated by Docker Inc.
Docker Hub and a Docker registry are two names for the same underlying object; the term used depends on whether you are logged into Docker Inc.'s hosted instance
Docker Hub is the free open-source reference implementation while any other registry is a proprietary commercial product requiring a paid license per pull
A Docker registry stores container runtime logs and traces alongside images, and Docker Hub is specifically the observability side of that stack
questions.explanation: A Docker registry is any service that speaks the Docker Registry HTTP API v2 for storing and serving images; Docker Hub is the specific public registry that Docker Inc. operates. Other registries include ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, Harbor, and self-hosted `registry:2`. Hub and registry are not synonyms — Hub is one registry among many. The reference open-source implementation (`distribution/distribution`) is Apache-2 licensed; commercial and free registries both exist, so the licensing framing is wrong. Registries do not store container logs; log storage is handled by logging drivers or external systems.

questions.q: A container must be capped at 256 MB of memory and half a CPU core. Which pair of `docker run` flags achieves that correctly?
choices: --memory=256m --cpus=0.5
--mem-limit --cpu-quota=50
--ram=256mb --cpu=half
--memory=256 --cpu-shares=0.5
questions.explanation: `--memory=256m` sets a hard 256 MiB memory cap (container is OOM-killed above it) and `--cpus=0.5` maps to a CPU quota equal to half a core — the canonical modern syntax. `--mem-limit` is not a real flag; the flag is `--memory`. `--ram` and `--cpu=half` are also invented; Docker does not accept English words for CPU fractions. `--memory=256` without a suffix means 256 bytes and would fail validation, and `--cpu-shares` is a relative weight, not an absolute core-fraction cap, so 0.5 there does not produce a half-core limit.
